title: Google Brain "cat" paper
description: A 1-billion-connection network trained on 16,000 CPU cores with 10 million unlabeled YouTube frames developed neurons that responded selectively to cats and human faces.
capabilityNote: Showed large-scale unsupervised learning could find high-level concepts, but its ImageNet-22k accuracy (~15.8%) was low in absolute terms; "Google's brain learned to find cats" overstated it.

sources.title: Building High-Level Features Using Large Scale Unsupervised Learning

title: AlexNet
description: An 8-layer convolutional network trained on two NVIDIA GTX 580 GPUs with ReLU and dropout. It won ILSVRC-2012 with 15.3% top-5 error against 26.2% for the runner-up.
capabilityNote: Showed that GPUs, large labeled datasets and deep CNNs beat hand-engineered vision features by a wide margin; commonly treated as the start of the deep learning boom.

sources.title: ImageNet Classification with Deep Convolutional Neural Networks (NeurIPS 2012)

title: ImageNet 2012 challenge result (ILSVRC-2012)
description: The 2012 ImageNet Large Scale Visual Recognition Challenge results showed a deep CNN at 15.3% top-5 error, about 11 points ahead of the next entry. The 2010–2011 winners had used SIFT/Fisher-vector pipelines at about 26–28%.
capabilityNote: A benchmark result on 1,000 object classes, not general visual understanding, but the size of the gap moved the field to deep learning within about two years.

sources.title: ImageNet Classification with Deep Convolutional Neural Networks (NeurIPS 2012)

title: word2vec
description: Shallow neural models (CBOW and skip-gram) that learn dense word vectors cheaply from billions of words. The C code was open-sourced in 2013.
capabilityNote: Vectors captured analogies such as king − man + woman ≈ queen and became the default NLP input layer until contextual embeddings replaced them; later work showed they also encoded social biases.

sources.title: Efficient Estimation of Word Representations in Vector Space
Distributed Representations of Words and Phrases

title: Adversarial examples ("Intriguing properties of neural networks")
description: Showed that imperceptible pixel changes can make state-of-the-art image classifiers misclassify with high confidence. Goodfellow et al.'s fast gradient sign method followed in December 2014.
capabilityNote: The first strong reality check on "superhuman" vision: high benchmark accuracy did not mean human-like robustness.

title: Deep Q-Network plays Atari
description: A CNN combined with Q-learning and experience replay learned Atari 2600 games directly from pixels and score. The 2015 Nature version covered 49 games.
capabilityNote: One architecture reached >75% of a professional tester's score on 29 of 49 games, but it failed badly on sparse-reward games like Montezuma's Revenge and needed tens of millions of frames per game.

sources.title: Playing Atari with Deep Reinforcement Learning
Human-level control through deep reinforcement learning

majorUpdates.title: Nature paper
majorUpdates.summary: Extended to 49 Atari games with one set of hyperparameters.

title: Google acquires DeepMind
creators: DeepMind (Demis Hassabis, Shane Legg, Mustafa Suleyman)
description: Google bought London-based DeepMind; reported prices range from roughly $400M to $650M depending on the outlet.
capabilityNote: Signalled that Big Tech was buying deep learning talent and set up the DQN, AlphaGo and AlphaFold lineage.

title: Generative Adversarial Networks
description: A generator and a discriminator are trained against each other so the generator learns to produce realistic samples.
capabilityNote: The 2014 samples were blurry, low-resolution digits, faces and CIFAR images; photorealistic faces took until StyleGAN (2018–19), training was notoriously unstable, and diffusion models largely replaced GANs after 2021.

title: Attention for neural machine translation
description: Added a learned soft alignment ("attention") over encoder states to RNN encoder-decoders for translation.
capabilityNote: Removed the fixed-length bottleneck so long sentences degraded less; the direct ancestor of the Transformer.

sources.title: Neural Machine Translation by Jointly Learning to Align and Translate

title: Sequence to Sequence Learning
description: A deep LSTM encoder-decoder that maps an input sequence to an output sequence, reaching 34.8 BLEU on WMT'14 English→French.
capabilityNote: Showed end-to-end neural translation could compete with phrase-based statistical MT and became the template for neural translation, summarization and chatbots.

sources.title: Sequence to Sequence Learning with Neural Networks

title: VGGNet and GoogLeNet (ILSVRC 2014)
description: Two deeper successors to AlexNet: VGG's 16–19-layer stacks of 3×3 convolutions and Google's 22-layer Inception network, which won ILSVRC-2014 classification with 6.67% top-5 error.
capabilityNote: VGG features became standard backbones for detection and style transfer; GoogLeNet used about 12× fewer parameters than AlexNet, showing architecture efficiency mattered as well as size.

title: Adam optimizer
description: An adaptive-learning-rate optimizer combining momentum with per-parameter scaling.
capabilityNote: Became the default optimizer for most deep learning, including Transformers via the AdamW variant.

sources.title: Adam: A Method for Stochastic Optimization

title: "Surpassing human-level performance" on ImageNet
description: Microsoft reported 4.94% top-5 error on ImageNet, below the ~5.1% "human" error estimated by a single annotator.
capabilityNote: "Surpasses humans" meant one person's estimate on a 1,000-class benchmark full of fine-grained dog breeds, not general visual understanding; adversarial examples showed the same models were brittle.

title: Keras
description: A high-level Python API for neural networks, first on Theano, that became TensorFlow's official high-level API.
capabilityNote: A few lines of code could define and train a CNN, bringing deep learning within reach of students and non-specialists.

majorUpdates.title: Default API in TensorFlow 2.0
majorUpdates.summary: tf.keras became TensorFlow's default interface.

title: IBM Watson Health (Watson for Oncology)
description: IBM launched a Watson Health unit and marketed its Jeopardy-winning brand as an AI system that would recommend cancer treatments. It sold the data and analytics assets to Francisco Partners in January 2022.
capabilityNote: STAT found only a few dozen hospitals had adopted it, and internal documents showed "unsafe and incorrect" recommendations traced to training on a small number of synthetic cases; MD Anderson benched its project in 2017.

majorUpdates.title: MD Anderson benches Watson
majorUpdates.summary: The flagship oncology partnership was put on hold.

majorUpdates.title: Unsafe recommendations reported
majorUpdates.summary: STAT reported internal documents showing unsafe and incorrect treatment advice.

majorUpdates.title: Assets sold
majorUpdates.summary: IBM sold Watson Health data and analytics assets to Francisco Partners (later Merative).

title: TensorFlow
creators: Google Brain (Jeff Dean, Rajat Monga et al.)
description: Google open-sourced its dataflow-graph ML framework under Apache 2.0; it scaled from phones to datacenters and later TPUs.
capabilityNote: Established the open-source deep learning framework as a standard layer and dominated industry through about 2018 before PyTorch overtook it in research.

majorUpdates.title: TensorFlow 2.0
majorUpdates.summary: Eager execution and Keras as the default high-level API.

title: ResNet (Deep Residual Learning)
description: Residual (skip) connections made networks of 152+ layers trainable, reaching 3.57% top-5 error and winning ILSVRC and COCO 2015.
capabilityNote: The residual connection became a universal building block, including inside every Transformer.

sources.title: Deep Residual Learning for Image Recognition

title: OpenAI founded
description: OpenAI launched as a non-profit research lab with $1B in pledged backing.
capabilityNote: No products at founding; it changed who builds frontier AI and restructured into a capped-profit company in 2019.

title: AlphaGo
description: Policy and value networks trained on human games plus self-play reinforcement learning, combined with Monte Carlo tree search. It had beaten European champion Fan Hui 5–0 in October 2015.
capabilityNote: The first program to beat a professional Go player on a full board without handicap; it relied on large TPU/GPU compute and was specific to Go.

sources.title: Mastering the game of Go with deep neural networks and tree search

title: AlphaGo vs Lee Sedol (Move 37)
description: AlphaGo beat Lee Sedol 4–1 in Seoul. Its Move 37 in Game 2 was first judged a mistake by commentators and then called creative.
capabilityNote: The public "AI creativity" moment; Lee's Move 78 in Game 4 produced AlphaGo's only loss, showing it could still be derailed by an unexpected move.

title: Microsoft Tay
description: A Twitter chatbot that learned from user interactions. Coordinated users got it to post racist and offensive tweets, and Microsoft pulled it within about a day.
capabilityNote: Microsoft apologised and said it had made "a critical oversight for this specific attack"; an early lesson that learning from open user input is an attack surface.

title: Sophia (Hanson Robotics)
description: A humanoid animatronic presented at conferences and on TV as a conversational AI; Saudi Arabia granted it "citizenship" in October 2017.
capabilityNote: Relied on scripted and operator-assisted dialogue; Yann LeCun called it a puppet and "Potemkin AI".

title: Google TPU v1
description: An 8-bit inference chip with a 256×256 systolic matrix unit, announced at Google I/O after running in Google datacenters since 2015.
capabilityNote: Google's 2017 paper reported 15–30× faster inference and 30–80× better performance per watt than contemporary CPUs and GPUs; it started the custom AI accelerator era.

sources.title: In-Datacenter Performance Analysis of a Tensor Processing Unit

title: WaveNet
description: An autoregressive dilated-convolution model that generated raw audio waveforms one sample at a time.
capabilityNote: Its speech was rated far more natural than earlier text-to-speech, but the original was too slow for production until Parallel WaveNet (Nov 2017).

sources.title: WaveNet: A Generative Model for Raw Audio

title: Google Neural Machine Translation
description: An 8-layer LSTM sequence-to-sequence model with attention replaced phrase-based statistical translation in Google Translate, starting with Chinese→English.
capabilityNote: Google reported large error reductions in human side-by-side ratings, but translation still failed on rare words, long documents and idioms.

sources.title: NYT Magazine, The Great A.I. Awakening

title: Microsoft "human parity" in speech recognition
description: Microsoft reported a 5.9% word error rate on the Switchboard telephone benchmark, matching professional transcribers on that test.
capabilityNote: "Parity" held on one benchmark; real-world accents, noise and far-field audio stayed much harder.

sources.title: Achieving Human Parity in Conversational Speech Recognition

title: PyTorch
description: A Python-first, eager-execution deep learning framework descended from Lua Torch. Code dates to 2016; the widely cited public release is January 2017.
capabilityNote: Became the dominant research framework by about 2019–2020 and the base for Hugging Face Transformers, GPT-Neo and Stable Diffusion.

majorUpdates.title: Caffe2 merged into PyTorch
majorUpdates.summary: Facebook folded its production framework into PyTorch.

majorUpdates.title: PyTorch Foundation
majorUpdates.summary: Governance moved to a Linux Foundation project.

majorUpdates.title: PyTorch 2.0
majorUpdates.summary: Added torch.compile, which uses Triton for generated kernels.

title: Self-driving car timelines (Tesla, Ford and others)
description: From 2015 to 2021 industry leaders repeatedly promised full autonomy or robotaxi fleets within one to five years.
capabilityNote: Musk predicted complete autonomy "in approximately two years" (Dec 2015) and over a million robotaxis by 2020, and Ford promised a Level-4 ride-hailing vehicle in 2021; none of these happened on schedule.

majorUpdates.title: Ford promises Level 4 by 2021
majorUpdates.summary: Ford said it would have a fully autonomous ride-hailing vehicle in commercial operation in 2021.

majorUpdates.title: "Over a million robotaxis"
majorUpdates.summary: At Tesla Autonomy Day Musk promised over a million robotaxis the next year.

title: NVIDIA datacenter GPUs (V100 and A100)
description: The Volta V100 was NVIDIA's first datacenter GPU with Tensor Cores for mixed-precision matrix math; the Ampere A100 followed in May 2020.
capabilityNote: V100 clusters trained BERT, GPT-2 and GPT-3; the A100 became the standard training chip for 2021–2022 models.

majorUpdates.title: NVIDIA A100 (Ampere)
majorUpdates.summary: Third-generation Tensor Cores, TF32/BF16 and multi-instance GPU.

title: Deep RL from Human Preferences (RLHF)
description: Trained a reward model from human pairwise comparisons of agent behaviour and optimized agents against it; for example, a simulated robot learned a backflip.
capabilityNote: Little noticed at the time, it became the root of the preference-tuning used for InstructGPT and ChatGPT.

sources.title: Deep Reinforcement Learning from Human Preferences

title: Transformer ("Attention Is All You Need")
description: A sequence model built entirely on self-attention, with no recurrence. It set a WMT'14 English→German record of 28.4 BLEU at lower training cost.
capabilityNote: Presented in 2017 as a translation improvement; its parallelizable training made scaling practical, and it became the architecture of BERT, GPT, T5, ViT, CLIP and DALL·E.

title: Proximal Policy Optimization
description: A simple, stable policy-gradient method with a clipped objective.
capabilityNote: Became the default RL algorithm, used in OpenAI Five, Dactyl and RLHF fine-tuning of language models.

title: AlphaGo Zero and AlphaZero
description: AlphaGo Zero learned Go purely from self-play and beat the Lee Sedol version 100–0; AlphaZero generalized the method to chess, shogi and Go from the rules alone.
capabilityNote: Showed human data was not needed in perfectly simulable, rules-known games; the 2017 chess result was disputed because Stockfish ran under restricted conditions, and self-play needed thousands of TPUs.

majorUpdates.title: AlphaZero preprint
majorUpdates.summary: One algorithm mastered chess, shogi and Go.

majorUpdates.title: AlphaZero Science paper
majorUpdates.summary: More matches addressed criticism of the Stockfish settings.

majorUpdates.title: MuZero
majorUpdates.summary: Planning with a learned model, without being given the game rules.

sources.title: Mastering the game of Go without human knowledge

title: Deepfakes
description: Autoencoder-based face-swapping was used to put celebrities' faces into pornographic videos without consent, reported by Motherboard in December 2017.
capabilityNote: The first mass-market generative-media harm; quality was crude by later standards, but it triggered platform bans and legislation debates.

title: ULMFiT
description: Pretrain an LSTM language model, then fine-tune it for classification with discriminative learning rates; released open source in fastai.
capabilityNote: Showed transfer learning ("ImageNet for NLP") worked with very few labeled examples.

sources.title: Universal Language Model Fine-tuning for Text Classification

title: Gender Shades
description: An audit of commercial gender classifiers from IBM, Microsoft and Face++ across skin tone and gender.
capabilityNote: Error rates reached ~34.7% for darker-skinned women versus ≤0.8% for lighter-skinned men; aggregate accuracy hid disparate failures, and vendors changed their systems in response.

title: Uber self-driving test car kills pedestrian
description: An Uber test vehicle killed Elaine Herzberg in Tempe, Arizona, the first pedestrian death involving a self-driving test car. The NTSB found the system detected her but failed to classify her or predict her path, and automatic emergency braking was disabled.
capabilityNote: A reality check on self-driving timelines; Uber sold ATG to Aurora in December 2020.

title: GLUE benchmark
description: A multi-task benchmark with a public leaderboard for natural language understanding.
capabilityNote: Models passed the "human baseline" within about a year, prompting SuperGLUE in 2019; an early case of benchmarks saturating faster than real understanding improved.

title: Google Duplex
description: An AI phone agent, demoed at Google I/O, that booked restaurant and salon appointments with human-sounding speech including "um" and "mm-hmm".
capabilityNote: In May 2019 Google told the NYT that about 25% of calls started with a human in a call center and about 15% needed human intervention.

title: GPT-1 (Generative Pre-Training)
description: A 117M-parameter Transformer decoder pretrained on BooksCorpus and then fine-tuned for each task.
capabilityNote: Established generative pretraining plus fine-tuning, improving the state of the art on 9 of 12 tasks studied.

sources.title: Improving Language Understanding by Generative Pre-Training

title: OpenAI Five (Dota 2)
description: Five LSTM agents trained with PPO on massive self-play, about 45,000 years of gameplay by OpenAI's count. They lost to pros in August 2018 and beat world champions OG 2–0 in April 2019.
capabilityNote: Superhuman team play in a restricted setting (17 heroes in the 2019 matches); players later found exploits in the public Arena.

majorUpdates.title: Beats world champions OG
majorUpdates.summary: Won 2–0 against the reigning TI champions.

sources.title: OpenAI Five defeats Dota 2 world champions
Dota 2 with Large Scale Deep RL

title: BERT
description: A bidirectional Transformer encoder pretrained with masked-language modelling, released with open weights in November 2018.
capabilityNote: Set records on 11 NLP tasks and became the default NLP backbone of 2019–2020; later probing showed it often exploited dataset artifacts rather than reasoning.

title: Hugging Face Transformers
creators: Hugging Face (Thomas Wolf, Lysandre Debut, Victor Sanh, Julien Chaumond et al.)
description: Began as pytorch-pretrained-BERT and grew into a unified library and model hub for pretrained Transformers in PyTorch, TensorFlow and JAX.
capabilityNote: A state-of-the-art model loaded in about three lines of code; with the Hub it became the de facto distribution layer for open models.

majorUpdates.title: Renamed transformers
majorUpdates.summary: After a July 2019 rename to pytorch-transformers, the library took its current name.

majorUpdates.title: Diffusers
majorUpdates.summary: A sister library for diffusion models.

title: JAX
description: Composable function transformations (grad, jit, vmap, pmap) over NumPy, compiled with XLA.
capabilityNote: Became the framework for TPU-scale research at Google and DeepMind and underpinned EleutherAI's GPT-J.

title: StyleGAN
description: A style-based GAN generator that produced photorealistic 1024×1024 faces; thispersondoesnotexist.com went viral in February 2019.
capabilityNote: The first widely seen photorealistic synthetic faces, soon used for fake social media profiles; it worked well only in narrow domains such as faces, cars and cats.

sources.title: A Style-Based Generator Architecture for GANs

title: AlphaStar (StarCraft II)
description: Agents trained by imitation plus league-based multi-agent RL beat pros TLO and MaNa 10–1 in January 2019 exhibitions and reached Grandmaster on Battle.net by October.
capabilityNote: The January matches were criticized for superhuman click bursts and whole-map vision; the Nature version added APM and camera limits and ranked above 99.8% of players.

title: GPT-2 and the staged release
description: A 1.5B-parameter Transformer language model trained on 40GB of Reddit-linked web pages that could write multi-paragraph coherent text. OpenAI withheld the full model, citing concerns about malicious use.
capabilityNote: Coverage framed it as "too dangerous to release" and critics called the withholding publicity; the full model shipped nine months later, and its text lost coherence over longer passages.

majorUpdates.title: 355M model released
majorUpdates.summary: Second stage of the staged release.

majorUpdates.title: 774M model released
majorUpdates.summary: Third stage of the staged release.

majorUpdates.title: Full 1.5B model released
majorUpdates.summary: OpenAI released the full model about nine months after the announcement.

sources.title: Language Models are Unsupervised Multitask Learners

title: OpenAI LP and Microsoft's $1B investment
description: OpenAI created a capped-profit entity to raise capital, then in July 2019 took $1B from Microsoft with Azure as its exclusive cloud.
capabilityNote: Tied frontier model development to hyperscaler compute; GPT-3 was trained on Azure.

majorUpdates.title: Microsoft invests $1B
majorUpdates.summary: Exclusive Azure computing partnership.

title: Turing Award to Hinton, LeCun and Bengio
description: ACM gave the 2018 Turing Award to the three "for conceptual and engineering breakthroughs that have made deep neural networks a critical component of computing."
capabilityNote: Formal recognition that deep learning had moved from the fringe to mainstream computer science.

title: Pluribus (six-player poker)
description: Beat elite professionals at six-player no-limit Texas hold'em, following the heads-up Libratus in 2017.
capabilityNote: The first superhuman result in a multiplayer imperfect-information game; it used search and counterfactual regret minimization rather than deep learning, on a small compute budget.

title: OpenAI Dactyl solves a Rubik's Cube
description: A Shadow robot hand trained in simulation with automatic domain randomization manipulated a Rubik's Cube one-handed.
capabilityNote: The solution sequence came from a classical solver and the network did only the manipulation, with about 60% success overall and 20% on the hardest scrambles; OpenAI disbanded its robotics team in 2021.

sources.title: Solving Rubik's Cube with a robot hand

title: T5 and the C4 dataset
description: A text-to-text Transformer of up to 11B parameters trained on C4, about 750GB of filtered Common Crawl.
capabilityNote: Made cleaned Common Crawl a standard pretraining source; a 2021 audit found C4's blocklist disproportionately removed text by and about minority groups.

sources.title: Exploring the Limits of Transfer Learning with a Unified Text-to-Text Transformer

title: BERT deployed in Google Search
description: Google began using BERT to interpret search queries, affecting about 1 in 10 US English queries at launch.
capabilityNote: The first mass-scale production deployment of a pretrained Transformer.

title: Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models
description: Language model loss falls as a smooth power law in parameters, data and compute.
capabilityNote: Gave labs an empirical basis for betting on scale, starting with GPT-3; DeepMind's Chinchilla (2022) later showed Kaplan-era models were undertrained.

sources.title: Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models

title: GPT-3
description: A 175B-parameter decoder Transformer trained on about 300B tokens and offered only through an API.
capabilityNote: Could write, translate and generate simple code from a few examples in the prompt, but made confident errors and failed at arithmetic and commonsense; Sam Altman said "The GPT-3 hype is way too much."

majorUpdates.title: Private-beta API
majorUpdates.summary: Access opened through the OpenAI API.

majorUpdates.title: Microsoft exclusive license
majorUpdates.summary: Microsoft licensed GPT-3 exclusively.

title: Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models
description: Generates images by learning to reverse a gradual noising process, building on Sohl-Dickstein et al. (2015) and score-based models.
capabilityNote: Matched or beat GAN sample quality (FID 3.17 on CIFAR-10) with stable training; the basis of DALL·E 2, Imagen and Stable Diffusion.

title: EleutherAI and GPT-Neo
description: A volunteer collective formed on Discord to replicate GPT-3 openly; it released GPT-Neo 1.3B and 2.7B, trained on The Pile, in March 2021.
capabilityNote: Showed a non-corporate group could train and release GPT-3-architecture models, though far smaller than 175B.

majorUpdates.title: GPT-Neo 1.3B / 2.7B
majorUpdates.summary: First open GPT-3-style models from EleutherAI.

majorUpdates.title: GPT-NeoX-20B
majorUpdates.summary: 20B-parameter open model.

majorUpdates.title: Pythia
majorUpdates.summary: 16 models with 154 checkpoints each on identical data order, a standard interpretability testbed.

title: Vision Transformer (ViT)
description: A pure Transformer applied to 16×16 image patches.
capabilityNote: Matched or beat CNNs only when pretrained on very large datasets (JFT-300M); it unified architectures across vision and language.

title: AlphaFold 2
description: An attention-based network that predicts 3D protein structure from sequence and alignments, reaching a median GDT of 92.4 at CASP14.
capabilityNote: "Solving protein folding" meant predicting static single-chain structures, not folding dynamics or (initially) complexes, and it was weaker on disordered regions; Hassabis and Jumper shared the 2024 Chemistry Nobel.

majorUpdates.title: Nature paper and open-source code
majorUpdates.summary: Methods and code published.

majorUpdates.title: AlphaFold Protein Structure Database
majorUpdates.summary: Predicted structures released with EMBL-EBI.

sources.title: Highly accurate protein structure prediction with AlphaFold

title: "Stochastic Parrots" and Gebru's exit from Google
description: A critique of ever-larger language models covering environmental cost, undocumented training data, encoded bias and the illusion of meaning; Google's handling of it led to Gebru's and Mitchell's departures.
capabilityNote: The defining critical counter-narrative to scaling; the paper appeared at FAccT in March 2021.

sources.title: On the Dangers of Stochastic Parrots

title: The Pile
description: An 825 GiB open English text corpus built from 22 sources, including Common Crawl, PubMed, arXiv, GitHub and Books3.
capabilityNote: The first widely used open, documented LLM pretraining dataset; its Books3 subset later sat at the centre of copyright disputes.

title: DALL·E
description: A 12B-parameter autoregressive Transformer over text and image tokens that generated images from captions such as "an armchair in the shape of an avocado".
capabilityNote: Showed compositional text-to-image generation, but outputs were 256×256, cherry-picked with CLIP reranking, and the model was never publicly released.

title: CLIP
description: Image and text encoders trained jointly on 400M web image-text pairs with a contrastive objective; weights for smaller models were released.
capabilityNote: Zero-shot ImageNet accuracy matched a supervised ResNet-50, and CLIP became the text-image bridge for later generators; the paper documents typographic attacks and biases.

sources.title: Learning Transferable Visual Models From Natural Language Supervision

title: Switch Transformer
description: A sparse Mixture-of-Experts Transformer that scaled to 1.6 trillion parameters with constant compute per token.
capabilityNote: Headline parameter counts for sparse models were not comparable to dense ones; 1.6T sparse parameters are not equivalent to GPT-3's dense 175B.

title: LaMDA
description: A dialogue-tuned Transformer language model demoed at Google I/O talking as Pluto and as a paper airplane.
capabilityNote: Kept internal in 2021; it became notorious in 2022 when an engineer claimed it was sentient, a claim Google rejected, and it later underpinned Bard.

title: Anthropic founded
description: An AI safety company, founded largely by former OpenAI staff, that announced a $124M Series A in May 2021.
capabilityNote: No products in 2021; its founders included authors of GPT-3, the scaling laws paper and RLHF.

title: GPT-J-6B
description: A 6B-parameter open GPT-3-style model trained on The Pile with JAX on TPUs.
capabilityNote: The strongest openly downloadable GPT-3-style model of 2021, roughly on par with GPT-3 Curie (6.7B) on many zero-shot tasks by EleutherAI's evaluation.

title: LoRA (and QLoRA, PEFT)
description: Low-Rank Adaptation trains small adapter matrices instead of all model weights, cutting fine-tuning memory and storage.
capabilityNote: With QLoRA's 4-bit variant it let individuals fine-tune large models on one GPU, the biggest single enabler of the community fine-tune ecosystem (Hermes, Vicuna successors, image LoRAs).

majorUpdates.title: Hugging Face PEFT
majorUpdates.summary: Library packaging LoRA and other parameter-efficient methods.

majorUpdates.title: QLoRA
majorUpdates.summary: LoRA on a 4-bit quantized base, fitting 65B fine-tuning on one 48GB GPU.

sources.title: LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models

title: GitHub Copilot (technical preview)
description: An AI pair programmer in VS Code that autocompleted lines and whole functions, powered by Codex.
capabilityNote: The first mass-market LLM product for developers; a 2021 NYU study found about 40% of generated programs in security-relevant scenarios were vulnerable, and training on public code raised licensing disputes.

sources.title: Pearce et al., Copilot security study

title: Codex and HumanEval
description: GPT-3 fine-tuned on public GitHub code, introduced with the HumanEval benchmark; an API private beta followed in August 2021.
capabilityNote: The 12B Codex solved 28.8% of HumanEval problems with one sample and 70.2% with 100 samples plus test selection; capable but unreliable on long chains of operations.

sources.title: Evaluating Large Language Models Trained on Code

title: Latent Diffusion Models
description: Runs diffusion in a compressed autoencoder latent space with cross-attention conditioning on text.
capabilityNote: Cut the compute needed for high-resolution text-to-image generation enough to run on consumer GPUs; Stable Diffusion built directly on it.

sources.title: High-Resolution Image Synthesis with Latent Diffusion Models

title: Chain-of-Thought Prompting
description: Showed that prompting a model with worked, step-by-step examples improves its multi-step reasoning. The idea later became a training target for reasoning models.
capabilityNote: PaLM 540B with 8 chain-of-thought exemplars reached about 57% on GSM8K, versus about 18% with standard prompting.

title: InstructGPT (RLHF for instruction following)
description: Fine-tuned GPT-3 on human demonstrations and then with reinforcement learning from human feedback so it follows instructions. The recipe was the basis for ChatGPT.
capabilityNote: Labelers preferred outputs from the 1.3B InstructGPT model over the 175B GPT-3.

title: Chinchilla (compute-optimal scaling)
description: Found that model size and training tokens should grow roughly in step, and that earlier large language models were undertrained for their size.
capabilityNote: The 70B Chinchilla, trained on 1.4T tokens, outperformed the 280B Gopher.

title: ReAct (reasoning plus acting)
description: Interleaved written reasoning steps with tool actions such as search queries. The loop became the template for most later agent frameworks.
capabilityNote: +34 and +10 points absolute success on ALFWorld and WebShop over imitation and RL baselines.

title: Constitutional AI
description: Trained a model to be harmless using a written list of principles and AI-generated feedback in place of most human harm labels.
capabilityNote: Produced models rated less harmful and less evasive than the RLHF baseline in the paper's evaluations.

title: Sparks of Artificial General Intelligence
description: A qualitative probe of an early GPT-4 build. It was widely cited and also criticized for its non-reproducible method and its AGI framing.
capabilityNote: Anecdotal demonstrations only (drawings, proofs, code); no controlled benchmark.

title: Direct Preference Optimization (DPO)
description: Aligned models to human preferences with a simple classification-style loss, removing the separate reward model and RL loop. It became a standard post-training step, especially for open models.
capabilityNote: Matched or beat PPO-based RLHF on summarization and dialogue in the paper's tests.

title: SWE-bench
creators: Carlos Jimenez, John Yang et al.
description: A benchmark of 2,294 real GitHub issues from 12 Python repositories, graded by each repository's own tests. Its 500-task Verified subset (Aug 2024) became the standard yardstick for coding agents.
capabilityNote: At release the best model (Claude 2) solved 1.96%. On the Verified subset, reported scores went from 49% (Oct 2024) to 80.9% (Nov 2025); the two figures are not strictly comparable.

title: Scaling Monosemanticity

title: Writing (proto-cuneiform, Uruk)
description: Mesopotamian administrators began keeping accounts and records on clay tablets. This moved memory out of people's heads and into durable storage.
capabilityNote: Persistent, transferable storage of symbols and quantities. No processing of any kind.

sources.title: The Met, Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History: The Origins of Writing

title: Antikythera mechanism
description: A geared bronze device that modelled solar, lunar and eclipse cycles. It is the oldest known analogue computer.
capabilityNote: Predicted lunar phase, eclipse timing and calendar cycles from a hand crank. It performed one fixed computation and could not be reprogrammed.

sources.title: Freeth et al., Decoding the ancient Greek astronomical calculator known as the Antikythera Mechanism, Nature 444 (2006)

title: Ramon Llull's Ars Magna
description: A system of rotating paper discs that combined basic concepts mechanically to produce propositions.
capabilityNote: Enumerated combinations of concepts. It had no way to judge truth beyond the author's own rules.

sources.title: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Ramon Llull

title: Mechanical calculators (abacus, Pascaline, Leibniz's stepped reckoner)
description: Counting boards and the abacus let an operator do arithmetic by moving counters; Pascal's gear-driven adder (1642) and Leibniz's stepped-drum reckoner (1673) mechanised the carry and all four operations.
capabilityNote: Pascaline: addition and subtraction with automatic carry. Stepped reckoner: multiplication and division, though unreliable. Leibniz's 'calculus of reasoning' stayed on paper.

majorUpdates.title: Leibniz's stepped reckoner
majorUpdates.summary: Stepped-drum design extends mechanical calculation to multiplication and division.

majorUpdates.title: Leibniz publishes on binary arithmetic
majorUpdates.summary: Leibniz writes on binary notation and proposes a calculus of reasoning.

sources.title: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Leibniz's Influence on 19th Century Logic

title: Jacquard loom (punched-card control)
description: A chain of punched cards controlled which warp threads the loom lifted, so a pattern could be stored and replayed as a program.
capabilityNote: Replayed stored weaving patterns automatically. A fixed sequence with no branching.

sources.title: Computer History Museum: Punched cards, the Jacquard loom

title: Babbage's Difference Engine and Analytical Engine
description: A design for a general-purpose mechanical computer with a separate store (memory) and mill (processor), programmed with punched cards. It was never completed in Babbage's lifetime.
capabilityNote: Turing-complete on paper; nothing general-purpose was built. The Science Museum built Difference Engine No. 2 in 1991 and it worked.

majorUpdates.title: Difference Engine proposed
majorUpdates.summary: Babbage's earlier special-purpose design for tabulating polynomials.

sources.title: Computer History Museum: The Babbage Engine

title: Ada Lovelace's Notes on the Analytical Engine (Note G)
description: Notes to her translation of Menabrea's paper, including a procedure for computing Bernoulli numbers, often called the first published program. She also wrote that the Engine could not originate anything, only do what it was ordered to do.
capabilityNote: A program on paper only; no machine existed to run it. Also the first published sceptical statement about machine originality.

sources.title: Menabrea, Sketch of the Analytical Engine, with notes by Ada Lovelace (Fourmilab transcription)

title: Boole, "An Investigation of the Laws of Thought"
description: Treated logic as an algebra of variables that take the values 0 and 1.
capabilityNote: A formal basis that later made logic implementable in circuits. Theory only.

sources.title: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: George Boole

title: Turing, "On Computable Numbers"
description: Defined the Turing machine and the universal machine, and proved limits on what can be computed (the halting problem).
capabilityNote: Theory only. It set out what any mechanical procedure can and cannot compute.

sources.title: Turing, On Computable Numbers, with an Application to the Entscheidungsproblem, Proc. London Math. Soc. (1936)

title: Shannon, "A Symbolic Analysis of Relay and Switching Circuits"
description: Shannon's master's thesis showed that Boolean algebra can describe and design relay circuits. It was published in 1938.
capabilityNote: Made logic physically buildable; the basis of digital circuit design.

sources.title: Shannon, A Symbolic Analysis of Relay and Switching Circuits (MIT DSpace)

title: McCulloch & Pitts, "A Logical Calculus of the Ideas Immanent in Nervous Activity"
description: Modelled neurons as binary threshold units and showed that networks of them can compute logical functions.
capabilityNote: Theory only. The model had no learning rule.

sources.title: McCulloch & Pitts, Bulletin of Mathematical Biophysics 5 (1943)

title: Turing, "Computing Machinery and Intelligence" (the imitation game)
description: Replaced the question "can machines think?" with a conversational test, answered objections including "Lady Lovelace's objection", and proposed educating a "child machine".
capabilityNote: No machine was built. It defined the first proposed evaluation for AI and made a dated forecast for the year 2000 that was only partly borne out.

sources.title: Turing, Computing Machinery and Intelligence, Mind 59 (1950)

title: Dartmouth Summer Research Project on Artificial Intelligence
description: The August 1955 proposal coined the term "artificial intelligence" and asked for a two-month, ten-person study of machines that use language, form abstractions, solve problems and improve themselves.
capabilityNote: No breakthrough came out of the summer itself; Newell and Simon brought the already-working Logic Theorist. The goals listed stayed largely unsolved for decades.

majorUpdates.title: Proposal circulated
majorUpdates.summary: McCarthy, Minsky, Rochester and Shannon sign the proposal that names the field.

sources.title: McCarthy, Minsky, Rochester & Shannon, A Proposal for the Dartmouth Summer Research Project on Artificial Intelligence (1955)

title: Logic Theorist
description: A program that searched heuristically for proofs of theorems in Whitehead and Russell's Principia Mathematica.
capabilityNote: Proved 38 of the first 52 theorems in chapter 2 of Principia, one with a shorter proof than the original. The domain was narrow and formal.

sources.title: Newell & Simon, The logic theory machine, IRE Transactions on Information Theory (1956)

title: General Problem Solver (GPS)
description: A program that used means-ends analysis as a proposed general method for any problem that can be stated formally.
capabilityNote: Solved puzzles such as the Tower of Hanoi and simple logic proofs. Combinatorial explosion stopped it on real-world problems, so the "general" claim did not hold.

sources.title: Nils J. Nilsson, The Quest for Artificial Intelligence, ch. 5 (GPS; original RAND report P-1584, 1959)

title: LISP
description: A list-processing language with recursion, garbage collection and code-as-data, described in a 1960 CACM paper. It was the dominant AI language for about 30 years.
capabilityNote: Made symbolic programs (search, theorem proving, planners, expert systems) practical to write. It later spawned dedicated Lisp machines.

majorUpdates.title: CACM paper
majorUpdates.summary: McCarthy publishes "Recursive Functions of Symbolic Expressions and Their Computation by Machine".

sources.title: McCarthy, Recursive Functions of Symbolic Expressions and Their Computation by Machine, Part I, CACM (1960)

title: A* search algorithm
description: Best-first graph search with an admissible heuristic that guarantees an optimal path, developed for the Shakey robot project.
capabilityNote: Still the standard pathfinding method in games, maps and robotics.

sources.title: Hart, Nilsson & Raphael, A Formal Basis for the Heuristic Determination of Minimum Cost Paths, IEEE TSSC (1968)

title: Prolog
description: A logic-programming language in which programs are Horn clauses and execution is resolution theorem proving. It grew out of a natural-language question-answering project in Marseille.
capabilityNote: Made declarative rule-based programs and parsers concise. It became the core language of Japan's Fifth Generation project and of much European AI.

majorUpdates.title: Kowalski's procedural interpretation
majorUpdates.summary: Kowalski shows how Horn-clause logic can be read as a procedure, giving Prolog its theoretical footing.

sources.title: Colmerauer & Roussel, The birth of Prolog, HOPL-II (1993)
Körner et al., Fifty Years of Prolog and Beyond, TPLP (2022)

title: Minsky, "A Framework for Representing Knowledge"
description: Proposed "frames", structured stereotypes with default slots, as a way to represent knowledge.
capabilityNote: A design idea, not a system. It shaped expert-system shells and object-oriented knowledge representation.

sources.title: Minsky, A Framework for Representing Knowledge, MIT AI Memo 306 (1974)

title: SNARC (Stochastic Neural Analog Reinforcement Calculator)
description: A learning machine built from about 40 vacuum-tube "neurons" that simulated a rat learning a maze through reinforcement.
capabilityNote: Learned simple maze paths by reinforcement. Limited by its hardware and not scalable.

sources.title: Nils J. Nilsson, The Quest for Artificial Intelligence, ch. 4

title: Arthur Samuel's checkers program (and the term "machine learning")
description: A checkers program for the IBM 701 and later machines that improved by rote learning and by adjusting its evaluation function through self-play. Samuel's 1959 paper popularised the term "machine learning".
capabilityNote: Reached respectable amateur play. In 1962 it won a single game against Robert Nealey, which the press reported as beating a master; it never reached world-class play.

majorUpdates.title: IBM Journal paper
majorUpdates.summary: "Some Studies in Machine Learning Using the Game of Checkers" published.

majorUpdates.title: Game against Robert Nealey
majorUpdates.summary: The program wins one game against Nealey; press coverage overstates it as beating a master.

sources.title: Samuel, Some Studies in Machine Learning Using the Game of Checkers, IBM J. Res. Dev. (1959)

title: Rosenblatt's Perceptron (and the Mark I Perceptron)
description: A single-layer trainable classifier with an error-correction learning rule, demonstrated to the US Navy in July 1958. The Mark I hardware used a 20x20 photocell "retina".
capabilityNote: Learned to separate simple visual patterns into two categories. It could not learn functions that are not linearly separable. Press coverage in 1958 claimed it would walk, talk and be conscious.

majorUpdates.title: Psychological Review paper
majorUpdates.summary: Rosenblatt publishes the perceptron model.

majorUpdates.title: Mark I Perceptron hardware
majorUpdates.summary: Custom hardware with a 20x20 photocell input array.

sources.title: Rosenblatt, The Perceptron: A Probabilistic Model for Information Storage and Organization in the Brain, Psychological Review (1958)
The Conversation (2024), on the 1958 NYT perceptron coverage

title: ADALINE and the LMS (Widrow–Hoff) rule
description: An adaptive linear neuron trained with least-mean-squares gradient descent.
capabilityNote: Pattern classification and adaptive filtering. LMS became standard in echo cancellation and modems, one of the earliest learning algorithms in everyday deployment.

sources.title: Nils J. Nilsson, The Quest for Artificial Intelligence, ch. 4 (original: Widrow & Hoff, IRE WESCON 1960)

title: Cover & Hart, "Nearest neighbor pattern classification"
description: Proved error bounds for the k-nearest-neighbour classifier.
capabilityNote: A simple non-parametric classifier that became a basic machine-learning baseline.

sources.title: Cover & Hart, Nearest neighbor pattern classification, IEEE Trans. Information Theory (1967)

title: Minsky & Papert, "Perceptrons"
description: A mathematical analysis of what single-layer perceptrons cannot compute, such as parity and connectedness with bounded-order predicates.
capabilityNote: The proofs were correct for single layers. The book is widely credited with deflating neural-network funding in the 1970s, though historians dispute how much it caused.

title: Linnainmaa, reverse-mode automatic differentiation
description: A master's thesis, published in BIT in 1976, that described reverse-mode automatic differentiation, the algorithm behind backpropagation. It was not applied to neural networks.
capabilityNote: Efficient gradients of any composite function.

majorUpdates.title: BIT publication
majorUpdates.summary: The method is published as "Taylor expansion of the accumulated rounding error".

sources.title: Linnainmaa, Taylor expansion of the accumulated rounding error, BIT 16 (1976)

title: Werbos, "Beyond Regression" (backprop for neural nets)
description: A PhD thesis proposing that multilayer networks be trained by propagating derivatives backwards. It went largely unnoticed until the 1980s.
capabilityNote: Theory. Werbos applied it to neural networks explicitly in a 1982 paper.

sources.title: Schmidhuber, Deep Learning in Neural Networks: An Overview (sec. 5.5, history of backprop)

title: Hubel & Wiesel, receptive fields in cat visual cortex
description: Found "simple" and "complex" cells arranged in a hierarchy that respond to oriented edges.
capabilityNote: Neuroscience, not AI. It directly inspired the Neocognitron and later convolutional networks.

sources.title: Hubel & Wiesel, Receptive fields, binocular interaction and functional architecture in the cat's visual cortex, J. Physiol. (1962)

title: Statistical (HMM) speech recognition at IBM and CMU
description: Modelled speech as a hidden Markov process and trained the models from data instead of hand-written rules.
capabilityNote: This data-driven approach came to dominate speech recognition until about 2010.

sources.title: Jelinek, Continuous speech recognition by statistical methods, Proc. IEEE (1976)

title: Fukushima's Neocognitron
description: A hierarchical network of alternating feature-extracting and pooling layers modelled on Hubel and Wiesel. It is the architectural ancestor of CNNs.
capabilityNote: Recognised handwritten characters with some tolerance to shifts in position. It was trained without backpropagation.

title: Georgetown–IBM machine translation demonstration
description: A public demonstration of Russian-to-English translation on an IBM 701.
capabilityNote: Translated more than 60 pre-selected sentences using 6 grammar rules and a 250-word vocabulary. The staged demo fed forecasts of fully automatic translation within a few years.

sources.title: Hutchins, The Georgetown-IBM experiment demonstrated in January 1954 (AMTA 2004)

title: DENDRAL
description: A program that inferred molecular structure from mass-spectrometry data by applying chemists' heuristics. It is widely called the first expert system.
capabilityNote: Proposed candidate structures for a narrow class of organic molecules at expert level, with results published in the chemistry literature.

sources.title: NLM, Joshua Lederberg Papers: Computers, Artificial Intelligence, and Expert Systems (DENDRAL)

title: ELIZA
description: A keyword-and-template chatbot whose best-known script, DOCTOR, parodied a Rogerian therapist.
capabilityNote: Reflected user input back using pattern rules, with no understanding. Users still attributed understanding to it (the "ELIZA effect"), which turned Weizenbaum into a critic of AI.

sources.title: Weizenbaum, ELIZA—a computer program for the study of natural language communication between man and machine, CACM (1966)

title: SHRDLU
description: A natural-language dialogue system for a simulated blocks world that parsed commands, planned actions and answered questions about what it had done.
capabilityNote: Handled rich dialogue inside a closed world of a few dozen objects and did not scale beyond it. Winograd later abandoned the approach.

title: MYCIN
description: A rule-based system of about 600 rules for choosing antibiotics for blood infections and meningitis. It used certainty factors to handle uncertainty and could explain its reasoning.
capabilityNote: In a blinded 1979 evaluation on meningitis cases its recommendations were rated acceptable about as often as those of Stanford infectious-disease faculty. It was never used in routine clinical care because of integration, liability and data-entry burden.

majorUpdates.title: JAMA evaluation
majorUpdates.summary: Blinded comparison with infectious-disease experts on meningitis cases.

sources.title: Yu et al., Antimicrobial selection by a computer, JAMA 242 (1979)
Buchanan & Shortliffe, Rule-Based Expert Systems: The MYCIN Experiments (1984)

title: ENIAC unveiled
description: A general-purpose electronic digital computer, built for artillery firing tables and publicly unveiled in 1946.
capabilityNote: About 5,000 additions per second. It was reprogrammed by rewiring panels.

title: Point-contact transistor
description: A solid-state amplifier and switch that replaced vacuum tubes.
capabilityNote: Made reliable, dense and cheap digital logic possible; it underlies all later compute scaling.

sources.title: Computer History Museum: Invention of the point-contact transistor

title: Shannon, "Programming a Computer for Playing Chess"
description: Set out minimax search with an evaluation function, and contrasted brute-force (Type A) with selective (Type B) strategies.
capabilityNote: A blueprint only. The same framework, scaled up, beat the world champion in 1997.

sources.title: Shannon, Programming a Computer for Playing Chess, Philosophical Magazine (1950)

title: Unimate industrial robot at GM
description: A programmable hydraulic arm installed on a General Motors die-casting line.
capabilityNote: Repeated taught motion sequences with no perception. It was industrially useful.

sources.title: Computer History Museum: AI & Robotics timeline

title: Shakey the robot
description: The first mobile robot to perceive its surroundings, plan with STRIPS and act, developed at SRI from 1966 to 1972. The project also produced A* and the Hough-transform line detector.
capabilityNote: Pushed blocks between rooms in a prepared environment of plain walls and simple objects, taking minutes to hours per action. LIFE called it the "first electronic person" in 1970.

majorUpdates.title: Stanford Cart crosses a room
majorUpdates.summary: Moravec's camera cart crosses a chair-filled room in about five hours, showing how hard perception and mobility remained.

title: Moore, "Cramming more components onto integrated circuits"
description: Observed that the number of components per chip was doubling about every year; Moore revised the rate to every two years in 1975.
capabilityNote: An empirical trend that held for decades and is the compute backdrop to every later capability.

sources.title: Computer History Museum: Moore's Law predicts the future of integrated circuits

title: ALPAC report, "Language and Machines"
description: Found machine translation slower, less accurate and more expensive than human translation. US funding for machine translation was cut sharply afterwards.
capabilityNote: An evaluation event: the first formal public check on AI claims, 12 years after the Georgetown–IBM demo.

sources.title: National Academies Press: Language and Machines (ALPAC report, 1966)

title: Lighthill Report, "Artificial Intelligence: A General Survey"
description: A review for the UK Science Research Council that found AI had not delivered the impact promised and singled out combinatorial explosion. A televised BBC debate followed.
capabilityNote: An evaluation event. The UK cut AI support to a few universities.

sources.title: Lighthill, Artificial Intelligence: A General Survey (1973), full text

title: DARPA Speech Understanding Research programme (Harpy, Hearsay-II)
description: A five-year programme (1971–1976) aimed at understanding connected speech with a 1,000-word vocabulary.
capabilityNote: CMU's Harpy met the 1,000-word target with a constrained grammar and cooperative speakers. DARPA judged the results impractical and did not renew the programme.

majorUpdates.title: Programme ends
majorUpdates.summary: Harpy meets the target; DARPA declines to renew.

sources.title: Nils J. Nilsson, The Quest for Artificial Intelligence, ch. 14 (Speech understanding)

title: First AI winter
description: AI funding contracted from about 1974 to 1980 after ALPAC, the Lighthill Report, the Mansfield Amendments that pushed DARPA towards mission-oriented work, and DARPA's disappointment with speech understanding.
capabilityNote: Results in toy domains had not carried over to real-world scale. Combinatorial explosion and missing common-sense knowledge were the main technical limits.

sources.title: Nils J. Nilsson, The Quest for Artificial Intelligence, on the 1970s funding contraction and speech understanding

title: R1 / XCON at Digital Equipment Corporation
description: A production-rule system written in OPS5 that configured VAX computer orders, in production at DEC from 1980. It was the first commercially successful expert system.
capabilityNote: Configured orders with high accuracy and grew to thousands of rules. Maintaining those rules became a major cost, a classic case of the knowledge-acquisition bottleneck.

sources.title: McDermott, R1: A rule-based configurer of computer systems, Artificial Intelligence 19 (1982)

title: Lisp machines (Symbolics, LMI)
description: Workstations designed specifically to run Lisp for AI development, sold by MIT AI Lab spinoffs from about 1980.
capabilityNote: Strong development environments, but by about 1987 general-purpose workstations and PCs running Lisp matched them at a fraction of the price and the market collapsed.

sources.title: Nils J. Nilsson, The Quest for Artificial Intelligence, on the AI winter and the Lisp-machine collapse

title: Japan's Fifth Generation Computer Systems project (FGCS / ICOT)
description: A ten-year Japanese national programme to build massively parallel inference machines with logic programming at the core, starting from Prolog. It ended in 1992.
capabilityNote: Built PSI and PIM inference machines that met the target of about 150 million logical inferences per second, and about 20 demo applications ran in 1992. None were deployed commercially.

majorUpdates.title: Final conference
majorUpdates.summary: Project closes with applications in demonstration form only.

sources.title: Körner et al., Fifty Years of Prolog and Beyond, TPLP (2022), FGCS section
FGCS project appraisal, Future Generation Computer Systems (1993)

title: DARPA Strategic Computing Initiative (and UK Alvey Programme)
description: About $1B over ten years for machine intelligence, including an autonomous land vehicle, a pilot's associate and battle management, partly in response to Japan's FGCS.
capabilityNote: Funded the Autonomous Land Vehicle and Navlab work and parallel hardware such as the Connection Machine. DARPA scaled back the AI goals from about 1987.

title: Cyc
description: A long-running effort, started at MCC, to hand-encode common-sense knowledge as logical assertions.
capabilityNote: Accumulated millions of assertions over decades but never reached the broad common-sense reasoning or self-directed learning its founders aimed for.

sources.title: Lenat, CYC: A large-scale investment in knowledge infrastructure, CACM (1995)

title: Brooks's subsumption architecture
description: Layered reactive behaviours with no central world model, in contrast to Shakey-style sense-plan-act robots.
capabilityNote: Produced robust insect-like walking and obstacle avoidance, such as the Genghis hexapod in 1989. It led to iRobot and the Roomba.

sources.title: Brooks, A robust layered control system for a mobile robot, IEEE J. Robotics and Automation (1986)

title: Second AI winter
description: From about 1987 to 1993 the Lisp-machine market collapsed, expert systems proved brittle and costly to maintain, DARPA cut its Strategic Computing AI goals and FGCS ended without commercial take-up.
capabilityNote: Expert systems survived in niche use under other names such as business rules. The label "AI" became a liability for funding.

sources.title: Nils J. Nilsson, The Quest for Artificial Intelligence, Part V

title: Hopfield networks
description: A recurrent network with symmetric weights and an energy function in which stored patterns become attractors, giving content-addressable memory.
capabilityNote: Recalled stored patterns from partial or noisy cues, with capacity of about 0.14N patterns for N units. Hopfield shared the 2024 Nobel Prize in Physics with Hinton for this line of work.

sources.title: Hopfield, Neural networks and physical systems with emergent collective computational abilities, PNAS 79 (1982)

title: Boltzmann machines
description: A stochastic recurrent network with hidden units and a learning rule for probabilistic generative models.
capabilityNote: Learned internal representations on small problems, but learning was very slow. The restricted variant (RBM) became practical in 2006.

sources.title: Ackley, Hinton & Sejnowski, A learning algorithm for Boltzmann machines, Cognitive Science 9 (1985)

title: Rumelhart, Hinton & Williams, "Learning representations by back-propagating errors"
description: Showed that backpropagation trains multilayer networks whose hidden units learn useful internal representations. The algorithm had earlier forms from Linnainmaa, Werbos, Parker and LeCun.
capabilityNote: Solved problems a single-layer perceptron cannot, such as XOR and parity, and learned family-tree relations. Data and compute limited it to small networks.

majorUpdates.title: PDP volumes
majorUpdates.summary: Parallel Distributed Processing (MIT Press) popularises the connectionist programme.

title: NETtalk
description: A backprop network that learned English text-to-phoneme conversion and drove a DECtalk speech synthesiser.
capabilityNote: Learned pronunciation from examples, reaching about 90% phoneme accuracy on its training text. Widely demonstrated, including on NBC's Today show.

sources.title: Sejnowski & Rosenberg, Parallel networks that learn to pronounce English text, Complex Systems 1 (1987)

title: LeCun et al., convolutional network for zip-code digits
description: A convolutional network with shared weights trained end-to-end by backpropagation on US Postal Service handwritten zip codes.
capabilityNote: About 5% test error on USPS digits. It led to commercial check-reading systems at AT&T and NCR in the 1990s.

sources.title: LeCun et al., Backpropagation Applied to Handwritten Zip Code Recognition, Neural Computation 1 (1989)

title: Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM)
description: A recurrent architecture with gated memory cells that addresses the vanishing-gradient problem Hochreiter identified in 1991.
capabilityNote: Learned dependencies over more than 1,000 time steps on synthetic tasks. By 2009 LSTM-based systems won handwriting-recognition competitions.

majorUpdates.title: Forget gates
majorUpdates.summary: Gers, Schmidhuber and Cummins add forget gates, the form most later systems used.

sources.title: Hochreiter & Schmidhuber, Long Short-Term Memory, Neural Computation 9 (1997)

title: Bengio et al., "A Neural Probabilistic Language Model"
description: Learned distributed word representations (embeddings) jointly with a neural network that predicts the next word.
capabilityNote: Beat n-gram perplexity on small corpora but was expensive to train. An ancestor of word2vec and later neural language models.

sources.title: Bengio et al., A Neural Probabilistic Language Model, JMLR 3 (2003)

title: Deep belief nets and greedy layer-wise pretraining
description: Stacked restricted Boltzmann machines trained one layer at a time and then fine-tuned, showing that deep networks could be trained. The "deep learning" label followed.
capabilityNote: 1.25% MNIST error without convolution, and better dimensionality reduction than PCA in the companion Science paper.

sources.title: Hinton, Osindero & Teh, A Fast Learning Algorithm for Deep Belief Nets, Neural Computation 18 (2006)
Hinton & Salakhutdinov, Reducing the Dimensionality of Data with Neural Networks, Science 313 (2006)

title: Decision-tree learning (CART and ID3)
description: Methods for learning decision trees from data, so that rules were induced from examples instead of from interviews with experts.
capabilityNote: Produced readable classifiers from tabular data, a way round the expert-system knowledge bottleneck.

majorUpdates.title: Quinlan's ID3
majorUpdates.summary: "Induction of Decision Trees" in Machine Learning 1.

majorUpdates.title: C4.5
majorUpdates.summary: Quinlan's successor to ID3.

sources.title: Quinlan, Induction of Decision Trees, Machine Learning 1 (1986)

title: Pearl, "Probabilistic Reasoning in Intelligent Systems" (Bayesian networks)
description: Graphical models for representing uncertain knowledge, with efficient inference by belief propagation.
capabilityNote: Replaced ad hoc certainty factors with sound probability and was used in diagnosis and fault-detection tools. Pearl received the 2011 Turing Award.

sources.title: ACM A.M. Turing Award: Judea Pearl

title: Temporal-difference learning and Q-learning
description: Sutton's TD learning (1988) learns predictions from the difference between successive estimates; Watkins's Q-learning (1989) learns action values off-policy.
capabilityNote: The core reinforcement-learning algorithms behind TD-Gammon and, much later, DQN.

majorUpdates.title: Q-learning convergence proof
majorUpdates.summary: Watkins & Dayan publish the convergence proof.

sources.title: Sutton, Learning to predict by the methods of temporal differences, Machine Learning 3 (1988)

title: Support vector machines
description: Maximum-margin classifiers that use the kernel trick for non-linear boundaries, grounded in statistical learning theory.
capabilityNote: State of the art for text classification and many benchmarks from the late 1990s to the late 2000s, matching or beating neural networks on MNIST in that period.

majorUpdates.title: Soft-margin SVM
majorUpdates.summary: Cortes & Vapnik, Support-vector networks.

sources.title: Boser, Guyon & Vapnik, A training algorithm for optimal margin classifiers, COLT (1992)
Cortes & Vapnik, Support-vector networks, Machine Learning 20 (1995)

title: IBM statistical machine translation
description: Learned translation models (IBM Models 1–5) from parallel text of Canadian parliamentary debates, without hand-written linguistic rules.
capabilityNote: Showed that data-driven translation was competitive with rule-based systems. It led to Google Translate's statistical system in 2006.

sources.title: Brown et al., The Mathematics of Statistical Machine Translation, Computational Linguistics 19 (1993)

title: Ensemble methods: AdaBoost, random forests and gradient boosting
description: Methods that combine many weak learners, usually decision trees, into one accurate predictor: AdaBoost (1995), random forests (2001) and gradient boosting (2001).
capabilityNote: Strong off-the-shelf accuracy on tabular data. AdaBoost powered Viola–Jones face detection and random forests powered Kinect's body-part recognition.

majorUpdates.title: Random forests
majorUpdates.summary: Breiman's ensembles of decorrelated trees on bootstrap samples.

majorUpdates.title: Gradient boosting machines
majorUpdates.summary: Friedman frames boosting as gradient descent in function space.

sources.title: Freund & Schapire, A Decision-Theoretic Generalization of On-Line Learning and an Application to Boosting, JCSS (1997)
Friedman, Greedy function approximation: A gradient boosting machine, Annals of Statistics (2001)

title: Netflix Prize
description: A $1M open competition to improve Netflix's rating predictions by 10% RMSE, using a public dataset of 100 million ratings.
capabilityNote: Won in 2009 with a 10.06% improvement by a large ensemble built around matrix factorisation. Netflix later said it did not deploy the full winning ensemble because the engineering cost outweighed the gain.

majorUpdates.title: Prize awarded
majorUpdates.summary: BellKor's Pragmatic Chaos wins with a 10.06% improvement.

title: scikit-learn
description: A Python library with one consistent API for classical machine learning, begun as a 2007 Google Summer of Code project and first publicly released in 2010.
capabilityNote: Made classical ML (SVMs, forests, boosting, clustering) routine for ordinary developers and data scientists.

majorUpdates.title: First public release
majorUpdates.summary: INRIA team ships the first public version.

majorUpdates.title: JMLR paper
majorUpdates.summary: Pedregosa et al., Scikit-learn: Machine Learning in Python.

sources.title: Pedregosa et al., Scikit-learn: Machine Learning in Python, JMLR 12 (2011)

title: TD-Gammon
description: A neural network trained by TD(λ) self-play to evaluate backgammon positions.
capabilityNote: Played at or near the level of top human players and changed expert opening theory; humans adopted its moves.

sources.title: Tesauro, Temporal difference learning and TD-Gammon, CACM 38 (1995)

title: Chinook (checkers)
description: A checkers program built on alpha-beta search and endgame databases.
capabilityNote: The first program to win a human world championship title, in 1994, after Marion Tinsley withdrew from the match through illness. In 2007 the team proved that perfect play is a draw.

majorUpdates.title: Checkers solved
majorUpdates.summary: Schaeffer et al. prove perfect play leads to a draw (Science).

sources.title: Schaeffer et al., Checkers Is Solved, Science 317 (2007)

title: IBM Deep Blue defeats Garry Kasparov
description: A massively parallel alpha-beta search system with 480 custom chess chips and a hand-tuned evaluation function beat the world champion 3.5–2.5 in a six-game rematch.
capabilityNote: Searched about 200 million positions per second and did little learning: brute-force search as Shannon's Type A had anticipated, 29 years after Simon and Newell's ten-year forecast.

majorUpdates.title: First match lost
majorUpdates.summary: Kasparov wins the first match 4–2.

sources.title: Campbell, Hoane & Hsu, Deep Blue, Artificial Intelligence 134 (2002)

title: ALVINN and CMU Navlab (neural-network driving)
description: A small backprop network that mapped camera images directly to steering commands, an early end-to-end learned driving system.
capabilityNote: In 1995 Navlab 5 steered for about 98% of a roughly 2,800-mile trip from Pittsburgh to San Diego. Humans handled throttle and brakes and took over in hard conditions.

majorUpdates.title: No Hands Across America
majorUpdates.summary: Navlab 5 steers for about 98% of a cross-country trip.

title: Apple Newton MessagePad (handwriting recognition)
description: A personal digital assistant marketed on its handwriting recognition.
capabilityNote: The first version's recognition was widely mocked; later versions with the Rosetta recogniser improved considerably. Apple discontinued the line in 1998.

title: Dragon NaturallySpeaking
description: The first consumer software for general-vocabulary continuous-speech dictation on PCs, based on hidden Markov models.
capabilityNote: Usable dictation after speaker enrolment and training. Accuracy fell with background noise and accents.

title: LeNet-5 and MNIST
description: A seven-layer CNN combined with graph transformer networks for document reading. The paper introduced the MNIST benchmark of 60,000 training and 10,000 test digits.
capabilityNote: About 0.8–0.95% error on MNIST. It was part of an NCR check-reading system that, by the authors' account, read a substantial share of US checks in the late 1990s.

sources.title: LeCun, Bottou, Bengio & Haffner, Gradient-based learning applied to document recognition, Proc. IEEE 86 (1998)

title: Viola–Jones real-time face detection
description: A cascade of boosted Haar-feature classifiers computed on integral images.
capabilityNote: Detected faces at about 15 frames per second on 2001 hardware and spread into consumer cameras for face-priority autofocus in the mid-2000s.

sources.title: Viola & Jones, Rapid object detection using a boosted cascade of simple features, CVPR (2001)

title: Microsoft Kinect (depth-camera body tracking)
description: A consumer depth sensor for the Xbox 360 with real-time skeletal tracking for games.
capabilityNote: Tracked 20 body joints at 30 fps by classifying each depth pixel into body parts with random forests. It sold millions of units within weeks and became a cheap sensor for robotics research.

sources.title: Shotton et al., Real-time human pose recognition in parts from single depth images, CVPR (2011)

title: Deep neural networks for speech recognition
description: Context-dependent DNN–HMM hybrids replaced Gaussian mixture acoustic models, following 2009 Toronto results on TIMIT.
capabilityNote: About 33% relative word-error reduction on the Switchboard benchmark (Seide et al. 2011). It was deployed in Android voice search in 2012.

majorUpdates.title: TIMIT results
majorUpdates.summary: Mohamed, Dahl and Hinton show pretrained DNNs beat GMMs on phone recognition.

sources.title: Dahl, Yu, Deng & Acero, Context-Dependent Pre-Trained Deep Neural Networks for Large-Vocabulary Speech Recognition, IEEE TASLP (2012)

title: iRobot Roomba
description: A consumer robot vacuum using behaviour-based control.
capabilityNote: Covered floors with reactive bump-and-spiral behaviours and no map in early models. It was the first mass-market home robot, with millions sold by the late 2000s.

title: DARPA Grand Challenges (2004 desert race to 2007 Urban Challenge)
description: A series of autonomous-vehicle prize races: a 142-mile desert course in 2004, a rerun in 2005 and a mock urban course with traffic in 2007.
capabilityNote: No vehicle finished in 2004; the best covered about 7.4 miles. Five finished in 2005 and six finished the roughly 60-mile Urban Challenge in 2007, on a closed former air base.

majorUpdates.title: Second Grand Challenge
majorUpdates.summary: Stanford's Stanley wins; five vehicles finish.

majorUpdates.title: Urban Challenge
majorUpdates.summary: CMU's Boss wins; six teams finish the course with traffic rules.

title: Stanley wins the DARPA Grand Challenge
description: An autonomous VW Touareg that combined lidar, vision and GPS with probabilistic state estimation and learned terrain classification.
capabilityNote: Completed the 132-mile course in 6 h 54 min. It drove a pre-surveyed desert route, not traffic.

sources.title: Thrun et al., Stanley: The robot that won the DARPA Grand Challenge, J. Field Robotics (2006)

title: Google self-driving car project disclosed
description: Google disclosed that its test fleet, started in 2009 with DARPA challenge veterans, had driven about 140,000 miles with occasional human intervention.
capabilityNote: Drove mapped routes with safety drivers on board. Timelines for driverless deployment given later in the 2010s slipped repeatedly.

sources.title: Google Official Blog: What we're driving at (2010)

title: Google Translate switches to statistical MT
description: A free web translation service built on phrase-based statistical translation trained on large parallel corpora.
capabilityNote: Gist-level translation for many language pairs at no cost. Quality was uneven, especially between distant languages.

sources.title: Google Research Blog: Statistical machine translation live (2006)

title: Amazon Mechanical Turk
description: A crowdsourcing marketplace for small paid "human intelligence tasks".
capabilityNote: Made large-scale human labelling cheap; ImageNet's images were labelled through it.

title: NVIDIA CUDA
description: A C-like programming platform for general-purpose computing on NVIDIA GPUs, announced in November 2006 with the 1.0 SDK in June 2007.
capabilityNote: Made GPUs programmable without graphics workarounds. Researchers then reported large training speedups for neural networks (Raina et al. 2009, Cireșan et al. 2010).

majorUpdates.title: CUDA announced
majorUpdates.summary: NVIDIA announces CUDA alongside the G80 GPU generation.

title: ImageNet dataset
description: A large image database organised by WordNet nouns and labelled through Mechanical Turk, with 3.2 million images at publication and about 14 million later.
capabilityNote: Enabled supervised training at scale and a shared benchmark. The 2010–2011 ILSVRC winners used hand-engineered feature pipelines with about 26–28% top-5 error.

majorUpdates.title: First ILSVRC
majorUpdates.summary: ImageNet Large Scale Visual Recognition Challenge begins.

sources.title: Deng et al., ImageNet: A large-scale hierarchical image database, CVPR (2009)

title: Cireșan et al., "Deep, Big, Simple Neural Nets" on GPUs
description: Plain deep multilayer networks trained with backpropagation on a GPU, using elastically distorted training images.
capabilityNote: 0.35% MNIST error with no pretraining. GPU CNNs from the same group won several vision contests in 2011, including traffic-sign recognition at IJCNN with better-than-human accuracy.

sources.title: Cireșan et al., Deep, Big, Simple Neural Nets for Handwritten Digit Recognition, Neural Computation 22 (2010)

title: First Loebner Prize (restricted Turing test)
description: An annual chatbot contest billed as a Turing test, with conversation topics restricted in the early years.
capabilityNote: Winning programs relied on ELIZA-style tricks such as typos and whimsy. Stuart Shieber criticised the contest for rewarding deception rather than intelligence.

sources.title: Shieber, Lessons from a restricted Turing test, CACM 37 (1994)

title: IBM Watson wins Jeopardy!
description: IBM's DeepQA, a pipeline of hundreds of search and language components with machine-learned answer scoring on about 2,880 POWER7 cores, beat Ken Jennings and Brad Rutter.
capabilityNote: Answered clues, received as text, from locally stored documents with no internet access, winning $77,147 against $24,000 and $21,600. IBM's later commercial Watson Health products underdelivered.

sources.title: Ferrucci et al., Building Watson: An Overview of the DeepQA Project, AI Magazine 31 (2010)

title: Siri launches on iPhone 4S
description: A voice assistant, spun out of SRI's DARPA-funded CALO project and bought by Apple in 2010, that combined server-side speech recognition with task-oriented dialogue over web services. Apple launched it as a beta.
capabilityNote: Handled scripted domains such as reminders, weather, messages and search, and was brittle outside them. It started the mainstream voice-assistant category.

majorUpdates.title: Siri iOS app
majorUpdates.summary: Siri Inc. releases a standalone app.

majorUpdates.title: Apple acquires Siri
majorUpdates.summary: Apple buys Siri Inc.

sources.title: Apple Newsroom: Apple Launches iPhone 4S, iOS 5 & iCloud (2011)
